newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grain - Limited China corn seen in region.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Limited China corn seen in region.

text.p: Southeast Asian buyers said on Wednesday they do not expect to benefit much from a pick-up in Chinese corn sales after some easing of its export ban, but surplus Chinese shipments of soymeal have arrived in Thailand. China is rumoured to have some two million tonnes of corn for export but it is not expected to sell more than several hundred thousand tonnes, Indonesian traders said.

"All said and done, I don't expect China to be a regular exporter. It will be exporting considerably less than the rumoured two million tonnes," one trader who last week met with Chinese corn dealers said.
He said his Hong Kong-based Chinese contacts had sold between 15,000 and 20,000 tonnes of corn to Malaysia in mid-December, but could not recall the price.
"The big question is how much China will export and whether it will be a regular seller," he said. "It will be presumptious to say at this stage that China will be a regular exporter."
The trader said Chinese exports were expected to be mostly to the Far East, especially Japan and South Korea.
Another trader said Indonesian corn prices were firmer on good demand. Corn was quoted at between 380-390 rupiah a kg in Jakarta, up from last week's 370-375 rupiah.
"Demand is good, and one feedmill has been taking up big volumes," said the trader from the key growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra where the harvest was progressing.
Traders said soymeal prices were stable at 795-800 rupiah a kg in Jakarta, and that several vessels were arriving or about to arrive in Indonesia.
"The market will be depressed as a consequence of the arrivals," one trader said.

Data from Belawan Port showed that the MV Da Feng arrived at the North Sumatra port last Sunday with 3,500 tonnes of soymeal from India, while the MV Nan Jiang arrived last Tuesday also carrying 5,897 tonnes of soymeal from India.
In Thailand, domestic soymeal prices dipped as the market is flush with almost four cargoes of soymeal diverted from China and Vietnam, trade and shipping sources said.
But demand remains robust. Agri-business giant Charoen Phokphand last week bought 15,000 tonnes of South American-origined soymeal for June shipment, they said.
Two trading houses were said to have diverted cargoes of Indian-origin soymeal from China after buyers there defaulted on the contracts.
"They are now selling around $297 per tonne, below the market prices of $303-310 per tonne. They ruined us all," said one trader.

"A big stock there was perhaps one of the reasons why the cargoes were sent to Thailand. China has bought a lot recently...It might be difficult for them to absorb any more supplies," said another trader from a major US trading house.
A trade source said one Bangkok-based trading firm also diverted one cargo of soymeal originally destined for Vietnam for Chareon Phokphand.
"Chareon Phokphand made the request in order to cover its short positions. This lot of soymeal has not affected the market," the source said.
Soymeal was quoted around 9.20 baht ($0.36) from 9.30 baht a week ago.
Buying interest on groundnut meals has been active due to high world prices of soymeal, trade sources said.
Corn prices were steady to firmer at 4.25-4.30 baht per kg from 4.20-4.30 baht last week.
"News that the government delayed zero-tariff corn import schedule did very little to lift the price," said a corn trader.
"Major players are those in frozen poultry export business which can get a full refund on import tariff of animal feed raw materials anyway," he said.
Trade sources said they have not heard of any import orders for corn this week.
In Malaysia, traders could not report any substantial grain or soymeal purchases over the last week.
"I think importers are still comfortable, with enough stocks," said a trader. "If the prices come down any further, they might be prompted to buy."

Traders in Kuala Lumpur said last week that importers will be in the market for one or two shipments -- meaning 50,000 to 100,000 tonnes -- of corn for February/March if they could buy below $150 a tonne C&F.
"Technically speaking, some buying should start by February as the stocks most have in Malaysia are for until the first quarter," said the manager of a flour mill.
The strong local ringgit against the U.S. dollar was also a concern, although traders said it was not major enough to affect the market significantly.
